name: Self-experimentation

card.summary: Testing a diet, supplement, routine or product on oneself and tracking results, which looksmaxxers use to find what changes their own skin, body or face.
card.note: Self-tested interventions carry their own risks, and a single person's results cannot separate placebo or chance from effect.

quick.overview:
Self-experimentation means trying an intervention on yourself and recording what happens. In looksmaxxing it shows up as personal trials of skincare routines, diets, supplements and training changes, with photos and measurements used to judge results.

It has a long scientific history, from Barry Marshall swallowing H. pylori in 1984 to Werner Forssmann's self-performed heart catheterisation, and it now overlaps with N-of-1 trial designs and citizen health science.
quick.how: People usually change one thing at a time, keep a log or standardised photos, and compare before and after. Formal N-of-1 frameworks add baselines, blinding where possible and repeat phases.
quick.risks: Risks depend on what is being tested; unsupervised use of drugs or extreme protocols has caused harm. Ethics bodies note that self-testers cannot be blinded easily and may over-record favourable results.

lead: Self-experimentation is the practice of testing an intervention on oneself. Historically it has produced notable medical findings, and today it is part of personal-health, quantified-self and citizen-science culture [1][2][3]. In looksmaxxing it is how many people test skincare, diet, supplements and training for their own appearance, tracking changes with photos, measurements or logs.

Researchers distinguish strict self-experimentation, where the investigator is the sole subject, from looser forms [2]. Methodological work describes N-of-1 and single-case designs that make personal trials more structured [4][5].

chain: Track skin, body or face with logs and photos
angle.text: People use personal trials to find which products, diets or routines suit their own skin and physique. The structure (baseline, one change at a time) is meant to make results easier to read.

infobox: N-of-1 trials, quantified self, citizen health science [1][4]

paras: The concept has no single formal definition. A strict reading requires one experimenter acting as sole subject; a looser one includes researchers who join volunteers [2]. S. C. Gandevia proposed that it counts when the experimenter would be named an author on the resulting paper [2].

Examples cited include Max von Pettenkofer drinking cholera broth in 1892, Jesse Lazear's fatal yellow fever self-infection in 1900, Werner Forssmann's self-catheterisation, Barry Marshall's 1984 ingestion of H. pylori (Nobel Prize 2005), and Albert Hofmann's 1943 LSD experiments [2][6]. The Nuremberg Code and Declaration of Helsinki shaped later ethical thinking, including the principle that researchers should not impose procedures they would not accept themselves [2].

Members of appearance and fitness communities commonly test routines, supplements and diets on themselves and post before-and-after photos or logs. Citizen health science literature describes this broader movement and its methods [1][8]. A Hacker News discussion of the history of self-experimentation in medical research shows the topic's wider appeal [7].

A 2016 framework paper described how single-case designs can be applied to personal health, with a case study in irritable bowel syndrome [4]. A 2021 paper argued that small samples and self-experiments have been behind some medical breakthroughs [9]. Ethics commentators note that self-testers may lack the target condition, may feel peer pressure, and may over-enthusiastically record results, while supporters say self-testers record symptoms well [2].
No studies found specifically on self-experimentation for appearance. Methodological work on single-case and self-experiment designs exists in personal health [4][5].

timeline.event: Max von Pettenkofer drinks cholera culture to test a theory [2].
Framework for self-experimentation in personalised health published [4].
